source_text: Non te terremus, qui nec timemus, sed velim, ut omnes salvos facere possimus monendo μὴ θεομαχεῖν. Potes et officio iurisdictionis tuae fungi et humanitatis meminisse, vel quia et vos sub gladio estis. Quid enim amplius tibi mandatur quam nocentes confessos damnare, negantes autem ad tormenta revocare? Videtis ergo, quomodo ipsi vos contra mandata faciatis, ut confessos negare cogatis. Adeo confitemini innocentes esse nos, quos damnare statim ex confessione non vultis. Si autem contenditis ad elidendos nos, iam ergo innocentiam expugnatis. Quanti autem praesides et constantiores et crudeliores dissimulaverunt ab huiusmodi causis? ut Cincius Severus, qui Thysdri ipse dedit remedium, quomodo responderent Christiani, ut dimitti possent: ut Vespronius Candidus, qui Christianum quasi tumultuosum civibus suis satisfacere dimisit: ut Asper, qui modice vexatum hominem et statim deiectum nec sacrificium compulit facere, ante professus inter advocatos et adsessores dolere se incidisse in hanc causam. Pudens etiam missum ad se Christianum in elogio concussione eius intellecta dimisit, scisso eodem elogio, aine accusatore negans se auditurum hominem secundum mandatum. Haec omnia tibi et de officio suggeri possunt et ab eisdem advocatis, qui et ipsi beneficia habent Christianorum, licet acclament quae volunt. Nam et cuiusdam notarius, cum a daemone praecipitaretur, liberatus est, et quorundam propinquus et puerulus, et quanti honesti viri (de vulgaribus enim non dicimus) aut a daemoniis aut valetudinibus remediati sunt? Ipse etiam Severus, pater Antonini, Christianorum memor fuit. Nam et Proculum Christianum, qui Torpacion cognominabatur, Euhodiae procuratorem, qui eum par oleum aliquando curaverat, requisivit et in palatio suo habuit usque ad mortem eius; quem et Anto(??)s optime noverat lacte Christiano educatus. Sed et clarissimas feminas et clarissimes viros Severus, sciens huius sectae esse, non modo non laesit, verum et testimonio exornavit et populo furenti in nos pala(??) restitit. Marcus quoque Aurelius in Gemanica expeditione Christianorum militum orationibus ad deum fectis imbres in siti illa impetrarit Quande non geniculationibus et ieiunationibus nostris etiam siccitates sunt depulsae? Tunc et populus adclamans duo deorum, qui solus potens, in Ievis nomine deo nostre testimonium reddidit. Praeter haec depositum non abnegamus, matrimonium nullius adulteramus, pupilles pie tractamus, indigentibus refrigeramus, nulli malum pro male reddimus. Viderint qui sectam mentiuntur, quos et ipsi recusamus. Quis denique de nobis alio nomine queritur? Quod aliud negotium patitur Christianus, nisi suae sectae, quam incestam, quam crudelem tanto tempore nemo probavit? Pro tanta innocentia, pro tanta probitate, pro iustitia, pro pudicitia, pro fide, pro veritate, pro deo vivo cremamur, quod nec sacrilegi nec hostes publici veri nec tot maiestatis rei pati solent. Nam et nunc a praeside Legionis et a praeside Mauritaniae vexatur hoc nomen, sed gladio tenus, sicut et a primordio mandatum est animadverti in huiusmodi. Sed maiora certamina, maiora praemia.
thought_title: Christians do not fear; governors should remember humanity
orientation: Tertullian is addressing Scapula directly, urging him to spare Christians and warning that persecution is contrary to the governors' own mandate.
pass_a_gloss: We do not frighten you, who also do not fear, but I would wish that we could make all men safe by warning them not to fight against God. You can both perform the duty of your jurisdiction and remember humanity, or because you also are under the sword. For what more is commanded to you than to condemn the guilty who have confessed, but to recall those who deny to torture? You see therefore how you yourselves act against the mandates, so that you force those who have confessed to deny. To that extent you confess that we are innocent, whom you do not wish to condemn immediately from confession. But if you strive to crush us, then already you are attacking innocence. But how many governors, both more steadfast and more cruel, have turned away from cases of this kind? As Cincius Severus, who at Thysdrus himself gave a remedy, how Christians should answer, so that they could be released: as Vespronius Candidus, who released a Christian as if a troublemaker to satisfy his fellow citizens: as Asper, who lightly harassed a man and immediately dismissed him and did not compel him to make sacrifice, having declared beforehand among the advocates and assessors that he grieved that he had fallen into this case. Pudens also dismissed a Christian sent to him in an indictment, when the shaking of it was understood, having torn up the same indictment, saying that without an accuser he would not hear the man according to the mandate. All these things can be suggested to you both from duty and by the same advocates, who themselves also have benefits from Christians, although they cry out what they wish. For also the secretary of a certain man, when he was being thrown down by a demon, was freed, and the relative of certain people and a little boy, and how many honorable men (for we do not speak about common people) have been healed either from demons or from illnesses? Severus himself also, the father of Antoninus, was mindful of Christians. For he also sought out Proculus the Christian, who was nicknamed Torpacion, procurator of Euhodia, who had once cured him with oil, and had him in his palace until his death; whom also Antoninus knew very well, having been raised on Christian milk. But also the most distinguished women and most distinguished men, Severus, knowing them to be of this faith, not only did not harm, but also adorned with testimony and resisted the people raging against us with a palisade. Marcus Aurelius also in the Germanic expedition, by the prayers of Christian soldiers directed to God, obtained rains in that drought. How often by our kneelings and fastings even droughts have been driven away? Then also the people crying out 'God of gods, who alone is powerful,' in the name of Jove bore witness to our God. Besides these things we do not deny a deposit, we adulterate no one's marriage, we treat orphans piously, we refresh the needy, we return evil to no one for evil. Let those who lie about the faith see to it, whom we ourselves also reject. Who finally complains about us under another name? What other business does a Christian suffer, except of his own faith, which no one has proved incestuous, which no one has proved cruel for so long a time? For so great innocence, for so great uprightness, for justice, for chastity, for faith, for truth, for the living God we are burned, which neither the sacrilegious nor true public enemies nor so many guilty of imperial dignity are accustomed to suffer. For now also by the governor of the Legion and by the governor of Mauretania this name is harassed, but only to the sword, just as from the beginning it was commanded to punish people of this kind. But greater contests, greater rewards.

choices.why: The Greek phrase is a proverbial warning against opposing divine will; rendered literally to preserve its force.
Meminisse with genitive means to be mindful of; 'humanity' keeps the abstract noun as in the source.
Literal rendering of the metaphor for being subject to authority and danger.

choices.english: you force those who have confessed to deny
choices.why: Keeps the active force of cogatis and the participle confessos as object.
rejected: you compel the confessed to deny

choices.why: Expugnatis is present indicative with a military sense; 'attacking' preserves the aggressive connotation.
Literal translation of the metaphor for being nurtured in Christianity from infancy.

pass_b_english: We do not frighten you, since we ourselves are not afraid, but I would wish that we could save everyone by warning them not to fight against God. You can both perform the duty of your jurisdiction and remember humanity, since you too are under the sword. For what more is commanded of you than to condemn the guilty who have confessed, and to recall those who deny to torture? You see, then, how you yourselves act against your own mandates when you force those who have confessed to deny. By this very fact you admit that we are innocent, since you do not wish to condemn us immediately upon confession. But if you strive to crush us, then you are attacking innocence itself.

How many governors, both more resolute and more cruel, have turned away from cases of this kind? Cincius Severus, for example, at Thysdrus himself provided the remedy of how Christians should answer so that they could be released. Vespronius Candidus released a Christian under the pretext that he was a troublemaker, to satisfy his fellow citizens. Asper lightly harassed a man and then immediately let him go, and did not force him to sacrifice, having declared beforehand among the advocates and assessors that he was grieved to have fallen into this case. Pudens too, when a Christian was sent to him, understood from the indictment that the man had been shaken down, and released him, tearing up the indictment itself, and refused to hear the man without an accuser, citing the mandate.

All these things can be suggested to you both from your official duty and by those same advocates, who themselves have received benefits from Christians, even though they shout whatever they wish. For a certain secretary was freed when he was being thrown down by a demon, and so was a relative of certain people and a young boy. And how many respectable men—for we do not speak of common folk—have been cured either of demons or of illnesses? Even Severus himself, the father of Antoninus, was mindful of Christians. For he sought out Proculus the Christian, nicknamed Torpacion, the procurator of Euhodia, who had once cured him with oil, and kept him in his palace until his death. Antoninus knew him very well too, having been raised on Christian milk. But Severus, knowing that the most distinguished women and most distinguished men belonged to this faith, not only did not harm them, but honored them with his testimony and resisted the people raging against us.

Marcus Aurelius also, in the German expedition, obtained rain in that drought through the prayers of Christian soldiers to God. When have droughts not been driven away by our kneelings and fastings? Then the people too cried out, "God of gods, who alone is powerful," bearing witness to our God in the name of Jupiter. Besides these things, we do not deny a deposit, we commit adultery with no one's wife, we treat orphans dutifully, we refresh the needy, we return evil to no one for evil. Let those who falsely claim our faith see to it—we ourselves reject them. Who, in the end, complains about us under any other name? What other business does a Christian suffer except that of his own faith, which no one has proven to be incestuous or cruel in all this time?

For such innocence, for such honesty, for justice, for modesty, for faith, for truth, for the living God, we are burned—something that neither the sacrilegious nor true public enemies nor so many guilty of violating imperial dignity are accustomed to suffer. For even now this name is harassed by the governor of Legio and the governor of Mauretania, but only to the sword, just as from the beginning it was commanded that such people be punished. But greater contests bring greater rewards.
notes: The source text contains two damaged passages: 'Anto(??)s' and 'pala(??)'. The first is likely 'Antoninus' based on context; the second is uncertain, possibly 'palam' or 'palatio'. The gloss renders them as 'Antoninus' and 'with a palisade' respectively, but the damage is noted here.

last_rejected.quote: bearing witness to our God in the name of Jupiter
last_rejected.source_quote: in Ievis nomine deo nostre testimonium reddidit
last_rejected.why: 'Ievis' is an error for 'Iovis' (Jupiter); the crowd bore witness to our God, not in Jupiter's name.
last_rejected.fix: bearing witness to our God in the name of Jupiter
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'in Ievis nomine deo nostro' means 'in the name of I(e)vis (Jupiter) our God'; translation matches source.

last_rejected.quote: we commit adultery with no one's wife
last_rejected.why: Source says they do NOT commit adultery with anyone's wife; English reverses the negation.
last_rejected.fix: we do not commit adultery with anyone's wife
last_rejected.ruling: English 'commit adultery with no one's wife' preserves the negation of 'nullius adulteramus'; no reversal occurs.

last_rejected.quote: and to recall those who deny to torture?
last_rejected.why: Source means “but they deny (the governor) to bring them back to torture,” not “recall those who deny to torture.”
last_rejected.fix: and they deny to bring them back to torture
last_rejected.ruling: 'negantes ad tormenta revocare' = recall those who deny to torture; standard object infinitive, not 'they deny the governor.'
